{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in real analysis}}
In the mathematical field of [[real analysis]], the '''Steinhaus theorem''' states that the [[difference set]] of a set of positive [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] contains an [[open set|open]] [[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of zero. It was first proved by [[Hugo Steinhaus]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Steinhaus|1920}}; {{harvtxt|Väth|2002}}</ref>

==Statement==

Let ''A'' be a Lebesgue-measurable set in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> such that the [[Lebesgue measure]] of ''A'' is not zero. Then the ''difference set''

: <math>A-A=\{a-b\mid a,b\in A\} </math>

contains an open neighbourhood of the origin.

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 
Let <math>A \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}</math> be a subset of positive Lebesgue measure. First, we consider the case where <math>m(A) < \infty</math>. In this case, it follows that the [[Indicator function|characteristic functions]] <math>\chi_{A}(x)</math> and <math>\chi_{-A}(x)</math> are contained in [[Lp space|<math>L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{n})</math>]] for all <math>1 \leq p < \infty</math>. Then <math> h(x) = \chi_{A} \ast \chi_{-A}(x)</math> is continuous on <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> (where <math>\ast</math> denotes [[Convolution|convolution]]) and 

<math display="block">
h(0) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\chi_{-A}(-y)\chi_{A}(y)\;dy  = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\chi_{A}(s)\;ds = m(A) > 0. 
</math>

Then since <math>h</math> is continuous and <math>h(0) > 0</math>, there exists an open neighborhood <math>U</math> of 0 so that <math>h(x) > 0</math> for all <math>x \in U</math>. But by definition of <math>h(x)</math>, <math>h(x) > 0</math> if and only if <math>x \in A - A</math>. Hence, <math>0 \in U \subset A - A</math>. 

Now suppose <math>m(A) = \infty</math>. We can write <math>A</math> as the following union: 

<math display = "block">
A = \bigcup_{R = 0}^{\infty}(A \cap B_{R}(0)), 
</math>
where <math>B_{R}(0)</math> is the ball of radius <math>R</math> centered at 0. By countable subadditivity, there exists at least one <math>R_{0}</math> so that <math>m(A \cap B_{R_{0}}(0)) > 0</math>. Hence, since <math>A \cap B_{R_{0}}(0)</math> has finite Lebesgue measure, by the first part of the proof, there exists a neighborhood <math>U</math> contained in <math>(A \cap B_{R_0}(0)) - (A \cap B_{R_0}(0)) \subset A - A</math>. Hence, the proof concludes. 
}}

The general version of the theorem, first proved by [[André Weil]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Weil|1940}} p. 50</ref> states that if ''G'' is a [[locally compact group]], and ''A''&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;''G'' a subset of positive (left) [[Haar measure]], then

: <math> AA^{-1} = \{ ab^{-1} \mid a,b \in A \} </math>

contains an open neighbourhood of unity.

The theorem can also be extended to [[meagre set|nonmeagre]] sets with the [[Baire property]].

== Corollary ==
A corollary of this theorem is that any [[Measurable group|measurable proper subgroup]] of <math>(\R,+)</math> is of measure zero.

== Applications == 
A special case of the Steinhaus Theorem (and the [[Lebesgue's density theorem|Lebesgue density theorem]]) deals with the existence of [[arithmetic progression|arithmetic progressions]] in a set of positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, let <math>E \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, for some positive integer <math>n</math>, be a set of positive Lebesgue measure. Then for any integer <math>N > 0</math>, <math>E</math> contains a finite arithmetic progression of length <math>N + 1</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof<ref>{{cite web |url = https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4328990/show-that-a-set-a-subset-mathbbr2-of-positive-lebesgue-measure-contains-t| title = Show that a Set <math>A \subset \mathbb{R}^{2}</math> of positive Lebesgue measure contains the vertices of an equilateral triangle | date=10 December 2021|website=Mathematics StackExchange|access-date=10 January 2026}}</ref>|proof=
Let <math>E \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}</math> be a set of positive Lebesgue measure, <math>\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}\}</math> be an arbitrary collection of unit vectors in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, and <math>\epsilon \in (0, (2^{N} - 1)^{-1})</math>. Also denote the <math>n</math>-dimensional Lebesgue measure by <math>m^{n}</math>. By [[Regular measure|inner regularity]] of the Lebesgue measure, we obtain a compact set <math>K_{1} \subset E</math> such that <math>m^{n}(K_{1}) > 0</math>, and by [[Regular measure|outer regularity]] an open set <math>U \supset K_{1}</math> such that <math>m^{n}(U) \leq (1 + \epsilon)m^{n}(K_{1}).</math>

Because <math>K_{1}</math> is compact, the distance <math>R = d(K_{1}, U^{c})</math> is strictly positive. Let <math>\delta \in (0, R)</math> be arbitrary, and consider the set <math>K_{1} + \delta a_{1}</math>. If this subset is ''not'' contained in <math>U</math>, then we would have 

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
d(K_{1}, U^{c}) < \Vert \delta a_{1} \Vert = \delta < R,
\end{align}
</math>
which is a contradiction. Therefore, <math>K_{1} \cap (K_{1} + \delta a_{1}) \subset U</math>. This means that 

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
m^{n}(U) \geq m^{n}(K_{1} \cup (K_{1} + \delta a_{1})) = m^{n}(K_{1}) + m^{n}(K_{1} + \delta a_{1}) - m^{n}(K_{1} \cap (K_{1} + \delta a_{1})). 
\end{align}
</math>

By translation invariance of the Lebesgue measure, we note that <math>m^{n}(K_{1} + \delta a_{1}) = m^{n}(K_{1})</math>, and so 

<math display = "block">
\begin{align}
m^{n}(K_{1} \cap (K_{1} + \delta a_{1})) \geq 2m^{n}(K_{1}) - m^{n}(U) \geq (1 - \epsilon)m^{n}(K_{1}). 
\end{align}
</math>

Since <math>\epsilon < 1</math>, we see that the measure on the left side is strictly positive, which means <math>K_{1} + \delta a_{1} \neq \emptyset.</math> Now for each <math>i = 1, \ldots, N</math>, define the sets <math>K_{i + 1} = K_{i} \cap (K_{i} + \delta a_{i})</math>. By a generalization of the argument above, each <math>K_{i}</math> is contained in <math>U</math>. Moreover, for each <math>i</math>, <math>m^{n}(K_{i}) \geq (1 - (2^{i} - 1))m^{n}(K_{1})</math> (a simple application of induction immediately yields this result) so that each <math>K_{i}</math> is nonempty. This yields a nested sequence of sets <math>\emptyset \neq K_{N + 1} \subset K_{N} \subset \dotsm \subset K_{1} \subset E</math>. Let <math>q \in K_{N + 1}</math>. Since <math>K_{N + 1} = K_{N} + \delta a_{N}</math>, <math>q - \delta a_{N} \in K_{N}</math>. Likewise, since <math>K_{N} = K_{N - 1} + \delta a_{N - 1}</math>, <math>q - \delta a_{N} - \delta a_{N - 1} \in K_{N - 1}</math>. Repeating this procedure iteratively and eventually denoting <math>p = q - \delta\sum_{i = 1}^{N}a_{i}</math>, we recover the finite arithmetic progression <math>\{p, p + \delta a_{1}, p + \delta a_{1} +\delta a_{2}, \ldots, p + \delta a_{1} + \dotsm + \delta a_{N}\} \subset E</math> consisting of <math>N + 1</math> points. Hence, the proof concludes. 

}}
